newsitem.title: USA: WALL STREET AGAIN COULD BOOST NYC REVENUES--MCCALL.
newsitem.headline: WALL STREET AGAIN COULD BOOST NYC REVENUES--MCCALL.

text.p: The New York State Comptroller Monday said New York City again might get a big boost from sparkling profits earned by Wall Street's financial houses, which last year contributed handsomely to its tax coffers.

"Given the extraordinary performance on Wall Street, we see the potential for significant additional tax revenues beyond the city's forecast in the adopted budget," said H. Carl McCall, in a prepared statement.

New York City ended its 1997 fiscal year on June 30 with a record, $1.3 billion surplus, largely due to Wall Street's big profits. Mayor Rudolph Giuliani based his new, 1998 budget on fairly conservative earnings estimates for this sector, projecting $5 billion of profits, a sharp fall from the over $11 billion they produced in calender year 1996.

However, the state fiscal monitor warned that even with the new, New York City Transitional Finance Authority, the city still will hit its debt limit in fiscal year 2000. The Authority, which was created to sidestep New York City's debt cap, was expected to start selling bonds in September.

As a result, McCall, a Democrat who last week decided not to challenge Gov George Pataki in next year's race, recommended that New York City, which now pays for all its capital projects by selling debt, look for ways that it could use non-recurring resources, like asset sales, for pay-as-you-go financing.

"If such strategies are successfully implemented, the resulting decreases in debt issuance would moderate future debt service burdens, ease pressure on operating budgets and would help preserve debt capacity under the existing debt limit."

He singled out the Republican mayor's plans for the sale of the New York Coliseum in midtown, saying Giuliani instead might be able to use extra revenues from Wall Street. Under a pact with the Metropolitan Transportation Authority of the State of New York, the city plans to use the proceeds of the sale of the Coliseum for general operating budget expenses. In return, the city would pay for the Transit Authority's capital program by selling the same amount of bonds. The Transit Authority runs the city's subways and buses.
